# Understanding actor reads

Reading people and agents from Glassfrog is handled by three closely related
commands — the `actors` directory, the `actors <id>` single read, and the
`assignments` list. This document explains why the surface is shaped the way it is:
why there is one unified actor surface rather than separate `people` and `agents`
commands, why discovery and drill-in are split, and why the same filling
relationship is read from two ends.

## Why one unified actor surface

Glassfrog's API offers `/people` and `/agents` as convenience aliases over a single
`/actors` endpoint. The CLI could have mirrored those with separate `people` and
`agents` commands. It deliberately does not.

The reason is that `--kind human|agent` selects either through the one endpoint with
nothing lost — `/people` is just `GET /actors?kind=human`. A second command would
fork the discovery surface for no gain. There is also a concrete advantage to going
through `/actors`: the dedicated `/agents` alias is gated behind the
`ai_integration` feature, while `/actors?kind=agent` reaches agents *without* the
gate. Routing everything through the unified endpoint means agents are reachable on
any plan, and there is exactly one place to learn the actor-listing surface.

The same logic shapes the single read: `GET /actors/{id}` resolves both `per_` and
`agt_` ids and is ungated, so one `actors <id>` command reads either kind of actor.
The CLI does not route an agent read through the gated `/agents/{id}` alias.

## Why discovery and drill-in are split

The slice is built on a find-then-read split. Before you can read an actor's
footprint or learn whom to contact about a tension, you have to identify *which*
actor you mean. The directory (`actors`, no positional) answers that — it turns a
name or a role into an addressable id. The single read (`actors <id>`) is the
drill-in that id feeds.

These are the same command branching on whether a positional id is present, but the
modes are kept structurally separate: the directory's filter flags (`--kind`,
`--role-id`, `--query`) are list-only, and `--include` is single-only. Mixing them —
a filter with an id, or `--include` with no id — is a usage error caught before any
request. This is deliberate: folding the per-id read or the footprint embed into the
flat discovery read would blur the split the whole slice is designed around. Each
invocation is unambiguous about whether it is finding actors or reading one.

## Why the filling relationship is read from two ends

An assignment maps an actor to a role they fill. That single relationship is
genuinely interesting from both directions, so the CLI exposes both — and keeps them
separate rather than conflating them:

- **`assignments <actor-id>`** reads it from the *actor* end — "which roles does this
  actor fill?" — default-embedding the role.
- The role-filler read reads the *same* `Assignment` resource from the *role* end —
  "who fills this role?" — default-embedding the actor.

Conflating the two would fork the two read directions of one resource. Keeping them
as distinct commands means each answers one clear question and embeds the side you
did not already name.

There is a third, narrower view too: `actors --role-id <id>` returns bare *actor*
records for a role (pure discovery — turn a role into actor ids), whereas
`assignments` returns the *assignment* itself, carrying focus and election. The
directory finds; the assignment read explains the filling.

## Why `assignments` has no `--include` and no filters

`assignments` exposes no `--include` flag and no filters at all. This is not an
omission — it reflects the endpoint. `listActorAssignments` already embeds the filled
role by default (the whole point of the read), and its only other include value
(`actor`) is redundant when you just named the actor. A flag here would add a knob
with no useful setting. Likewise the endpoint accepts no query filter beyond
pagination, so any client-side narrowing (by role type, name, or focus) would be the
CLI second-guessing the API. The command returns the actor's assignments whole.

This follows a consistent anti-speculation idiom across the CLI: a flag exists only
when a real API capability and a real consumer sit behind it.

## Design boundaries

- **Read-only.** None of these commands creates, invites, updates, deletes, or
  un-assigns an actor. Actor administration is placed out of scope; the slice is a
  pure read surface. The endpoints' `POST`/`PATCH`/`DELETE` operations are
  deliberately not surfaced.
- **No standalone single-assignment read.** The API exposes no `GET
  /assignments/{id}` (that path carries only administrative operations), so there is
  nothing to surface — and an actor's assignments are already complete in the list.
- **Explicit absence, never invention.** Where a field is unset — a role with no
  purpose, an assignment with no focus, a non-elected seat, a top-level role — the
  reads render an explicit-absence marker rather than a blank or an invented value.
  The CLI surfaces exactly what the API returns and no more.
